claims.text: Resistance is the ratio of the potential difference across a component to the current in it, R = V/I; its unit, the ohm, is one volt per ampere.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 9702 structural exemplar under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: V = IR links the potential difference V in volts, the current I in amperes and the resistance R in ohms; it holds at every instant, whether or not R is constant.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 9702 structural exemplar under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The resistance of a uniform wire is R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity of the material in Ω m, L the length in m and A the cross-sectional area in m².

verification.method: Authored originally for the 9702 structural exemplar under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Doubling the length of a wire doubles its resistance; doubling its diameter makes the area four times larger, so the resistance falls to a quarter.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 9702 structural exemplar under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Resistance at a point is V/I at that point, not the gradient of the I–V graph; only a straight line through the origin shows a constant resistance.
